diagnostic_evidence.quote: \min_{v(\cdot)}\int_{0}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{2}\langle v,v\rangle+\int_{\Omega}V\circ\varphi\right)dt
In this paper we restrict to the case $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with $\varphi$ being a volume-preserving diffeomorphism on $\Omega$, and with Jacobian having unit determinant.
Using the diffeomorphism $\varphi$ as a change of variables in the integral and the fact that the Jaconbian of $\varphi$ has unit determinant, we have the identity
be an arbitrary smooth variation of the point $(\varphi, v, \pi, k)$ on $\mathcal{C}$
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}+v\cdot\hbox{grad}\,v =-\hbox{grad}\,(p - V)
The pressure $p$ is determined by the divergence-free (volume-preserving) constraint $\hbox{div}\,v=0$.

issues.failure_explanation: The barrier term is <V o phi> = integral over Omega of V(phi(x,t)) dx. Every admissible phi(.,t) is a volume-preserving diffeomorphism of Omega with unit Jacobian and phi(Omega)=Omega, so the source's own change-of-variables identity gives <V o phi> = integral over Omega of V, constant in t and independent of phi: the term is constant on the whole admissible set and contributes zero to every admissible first variation. Admissible variations are delta phi = eta o phi with div eta = 0, eta.n = 0, and <grad V o phi, delta phi> = integral over Omega of grad V . eta = 0 for every such eta; yet the proof keeps this annihilated term and applies the unconstrained fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (the variation is expressly taken 'on C') to obtain a pointwise equation. The correct condition determines the delta phi coefficient only modulo a gradient, and grad V is exactly such a gradient, so the force term grad V o phi in th1 is spurious. The same fact appears dynamically in th2: the extra term -grad(p-V) is a pure pressure redefinition (p-V is the ordinary pressure, the source stating that p is determined by div v = 0), so (mod:eulereq) is literally (eulereq).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Couple the barrier so that its variational gradient has a non-vanishing divergence-free part (e.g. add the path term integral from 0 to T of V(phi(X_0,t)) dt for marked material particles X_0, or weight the barrier by a non-advected density) and re-derive th1 and th2, whose equations then contain a genuine non-gradient force; alternatively drop the obstacle-avoidance and pressure-control claims and state that (17) is the classical geodesic (Euler) problem.
issues.overall_effect: th1's third equation is not a necessary condition of the stated problem and its extremals are the ordinary impulse/Euler equations; th2's 'modified Euler equation' is the unmodified Euler equation. Hence the Remark's guarantee that optimal trajectories avoid S, the abstract's obstacle-avoidance claim, the conclusion's claim of controlling the pressure, and the interpretation of the simulations are all unsupported.
issues.title: Barrier term of the cost is invariant along admissible motions, so it cannot modify the flow
issues.why_classification: Every supported resolution either replaces the potential coupling and requires essentially new extremal equations and new experiments, or abandons the advertised obstacle-avoidance and pressure-control guarantees; no comparable version of the central result survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \Big\langle (Tv\circ \varphi)^{T} \pi + \frac{\partial \pi}{\partial t} + \text{grad }V \circ \varphi, \delta \varphi \Big\rangle
\Big\langle \pi, v\circ \varphi - \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} \Big\rangle - \frac{1}{2} \langle v,v \rangle
+ \langle k\, \text{div}\, v + V\circ \varphi \rangle \right]
\frac{1}{2}\langle v,v\rangle+\int_{\Omega}V\circ\varphi

issues.failure_explanation: The proof's own first-variation display gives the delta phi coefficient (Tv o phi)^T pi + d pi/dt + grad V o phi, so criticality yields d pi/dt = -(Tv o phi)^T pi - grad V o phi, the opposite sign from the stated conclusion. Independently, the extended functional pairs the kinetic term -(1/2)<v,v> with the potential term +<V o phi>, while the cost in (first:functional) is +(1/2)<v,v> + integral of V o phi; the two cost terms must carry the same sign for J to be, up to overall and multiplier signs, minus that cost. As written, critical curves of J extremize (1/2)<v,v> - <V o phi>, i.e. a potential well of depth V instead of a barrier, and adopting the sign computed in the proof would give the momentum equation -grad(p+V) rather than -grad(p-V).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change + <V o phi> to - <V o phi> in the definition of J; then the cost of (17), the computed first variation and th1's stated equation are mutually consistent and th2 is unchanged. The alternative repair (flipping the sign in th1's conclusion and in (mod:eulereq)) contradicts the cost in (17).
issues.overall_effect: The asserted correspondence between optimal solutions of (17) and critical curves of J is wrong, and the direction of the force in th1's third equation and in (mod:eulereq) is undetermined: with the equations exactly as stated the force grad V points toward the barrier (V maximal at S), i.e. it is attractive, not the 'repulsion' the Remark claims.
issues.title: Sign of the potential term inconsistent between the cost, the extended functional and Theorem 1
issues.why_classification: A single local sign correction in the definition of J makes the variational computation, the statement of th1 and the cost (17) consistent and preserves every stated equation and guarantee; only the informal 'repulsion' wording would have to be restated as cost-level avoidance.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \textbf{Assumption:} We assume from now on  that $\Omega$ has a boundary and the tangencial component of $v$ vanishes at the boundary.
together with the assumption that $\Omega$ has a boundary $\partial\Omega$ and $v$ vanishes at $\partial\Omega$
divergence-free smooth vector fields taking values on $\Omega$ which are parallel to the boundary
\int_{\partial\Omega} k\, \delta v \cdot n\, dS,
Our assumption is the minimal requirement to satisfy Stokes theorem in the proof of the main result as well as for numerical simulation purposes.

issues.failure_explanation: Three mutually incompatible boundary conditions are imposed: the Assumption requires the tangential component of v to vanish (so v is normal to the boundary and through-flow is allowed), the problem formulation and the curve space C require v to vanish on the boundary, and the Lie-algebra description requires v to be parallel to the boundary. The divergence-theorem step yields the boundary term integral over the boundary of k delta v . n dS, which contains delta v and not v, so the quoted reason is not a valid justification at all; the term vanishes only when delta v . n = 0 on the boundary. Under the Assumption as literally stated, admissible delta v are normal at the boundary and the term does not vanish, so th1's second equation does not follow (an extra condition such as k constant on the boundary would be needed), and the claim that this Assumption is the minimal requirement for Stokes' theorem is false.

failure_location.quote: where the last term vanishes since $v(x,t)$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$ and we deduce that

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Adopt one boundary condition (e.g. v.n = 0 on the boundary, or v = 0 on the boundary) in the Assumption, in C and in the proof, and justify the vanishing boundary term by delta v . n = 0 rather than by v = 0.
issues.overall_effect: The hypothesis set is inconsistent and th1's proof fails under the stated Assumption, with th2 inheriting the failure. The numerical section also lies outside the announced scope, using a periodic box ('points lying in the border of the square identified') although the paper expressly excludes that setting.
issues.title: Incompatible boundary hypotheses; divergence-theorem boundary term does not vanish as claimed
issues.why_classification: Standardizing to a single boundary condition is a local edit that makes the hypotheses consistent and validates the boundary-term step, leaving all statements and guarantees unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The function $V$  goes to infinity  near the obstacle and decays to zero at some positive level set far away from the obstacle $S$.
We consider $S\subset\Omega$ to be the regular zero level set defined by a scalar valued smooth function  $f$, for instance, used to describe obstacles as spheres or ellipsoids in the space.
\min_{v(\cdot)}\int_{0}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{2}\langle v,v\rangle+\int_{\Omega}V\circ\varphi\right)dt

issues.failure_explanation: For the proposed V = tau/((x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+(z-c)^2-r^2) one has V asymptotic to tau/(2 r s) with s the signed distance to the level set S = {|x-a| = r}; the integral over Omega of V dx therefore diverges logarithmically when S is crossed (the positive and negative parts diverge separately, so it is not even conditionally defined). Since the barrier term of the cost equals that integral, the cost is not finite for any admissible trajectory: problem (17) has no optimal trajectories at all, so the assertion that the potential 'ensures that such an optimal trajectory does not intersect S' has no content. In addition V is negative and unbounded below inside the sphere, so it does not penalize the enclosed region in any sense.

failure_location.quote: This ensures that  such an optimal trajectory does not intersect $S$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace V by a barrier with a weaker, locally integrable singularity at S (for example tau/|f|^(1/2)) and, if the enclosed region is to be excluded, by a potential that stays large on it; the avoidance guarantee additionally needs the non-degenerate potential coupling of ISSUE-001.
issues.overall_effect: With the barrier proposed in the Remark (and used in the experiment) the optimal control problem is ill-posed and the claimed collision-avoidance guarantee is vacuous.
issues.title: Proposed barrier potential makes the cost infinite and does not penalize the obstacle's interior
issues.why_classification: Weakening the singularity of the barrier potential is a local, routine change that makes the cost finite and the barrier meaningful, requiring no new argument or construction; the residual failure of the avoidance claim is the separate degeneracy ISSUE-001.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: even though we depart from divergence-free initial conditions
\hbox{div}\, v =0,
in order to obtain solutions with zero divergence.

issues.failure_explanation: For the stated data, du/dx + dv/dy = sin x sin y + cos y cos x = cos(x-y), which is not identically zero (it equals 1 at the origin). The system being integrated, (mod:eulereq), contains the constraint div v = 0, and the text asserts divergence-free initial conditions and 'solutions with zero divergence'; the experiment therefore starts outside the solution set of the claimed system, and the computed path is not a solution of (mod:eulereq).

failure_location.quote: using as initial conditions the functions $u(x,y,0) = - \sin y \cos x$ and $v(x,y,0)= \sin y \cos x$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the initial field by a divergence-free pair (for example u = -sin x cos y, v = cos x sin y, or the stated pair with the roles of x and y corrected) and re-run the experiment.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical experiment is not initialized with admissible data for the stated system and cannot illustrate the necessary conditions or the modified Euler equations as claimed.
issues.title: Simulation initial conditions are not divergence-free
issues.why_classification: Correcting the initial data to any divergence-free pair is a local, routine change that preserves the experiment's design and every guarantee attached to it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \Delta^{d} \phi (i,j)  = \nabla^{d} \cdot \nabla^{d} \phi
= \frac{\phi(i+2,j) + \phi(i-2,j) + \phi(i,j+2) + \phi(i,j-2) - 4 \phi(i,j)}{4 \Delta x^{2}}.
= \left( \frac{\phi(i+1,j) - \phi(i-1,j)}{2\Delta x}, \frac{\phi(i,j+1) - \phi(i,j-1)}{2\Delta x} \right)
X_{0} = X - \nabla^{d} \phi,
points lying in the border of the square identified

issues.failure_explanation: The stencil of Delta^d = grad^d . grad^d shifts indices by plus or minus 2, so it couples only grid points of the same parity class (i mod 2, j mod 2); the operator is block diagonal over the four parity sublattices and its kernel contains every function constant on each of them (four-dimensional on the periodic grid actually used). Hence the discrete Poisson equation Delta^d phi = grad^d . X is never uniquely solvable, contrary to the quoted claim. Worse, grad^d annihilates each such mode (for a parity indicator phi(i+1,j) = phi(i-1,j) = 0), so the defining constraint grad^d . X_0 = 0 is blind to grid-scale checkerboard components: a field with arbitrarily large continuum divergence satisfies it. The projection therefore does not deliver the 'zero divergence' outputs claimed.

failure_location.quote: With suitable boundary conditions, this scalar field is unique.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use a discretization without odd-even decoupling (a staggered grid, or a compact five-point Laplacian paired with matching first differences) and state uniqueness only up to the kernel of grad^d, which suffices because X_0 is then unique.
issues.overall_effect: The stated guarantees of the discrete Helmholtz projection (unique potential, divergence-free output) fail; the post-processing of the simulation does not establish incompressibility of the computed field.
issues.title: Discrete Helmholtz projection: odd-even decoupling destroys uniqueness and weakens the divergence constraint
issues.why_classification: Swapping the central-difference stencils for a standard compact or staggered pair and weakening the uniqueness claim to uniqueness up to constants is a short, local fix that preserves the method, the projection and its intended guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We integrated the $2$-dimensional version of equation \eqref{mod:eulereq} using a finite differences method
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}+v\cdot\hbox{grad}\,v =-\hbox{grad}\,(p - V)
The pressure $p$ is determined by the divergence-free (volume-preserving) constraint $\hbox{div}\,v=0$.

The result of discretizing the first equation in \eqref{mod:eulereq} using a finite difference scheme may result in a discrete vector field with discrete divergence, even though we depart from divergence-free initial conditions.

issues.failure_explanation: The system (mod:eulereq) is constrained: the pressure p is fixed at each instant by div v = 0 (equivalently by the pressure Poisson equation obtained by taking the divergence of the momentum equation), as the paper itself states. The described scheme contains no step that computes p at all and enforces the constraint only once, after the entire time integration, so the field it produces is not a solution of (mod:eulereq) but of the unconstrained momentum equation followed by one projection. Moreover, because the added term is the gradient grad V, any consistent incompressible time step (Helmholtz projection of the intermediate velocity) annihilates it completely; the reported deflection of the flow around the obstacle is therefore an artefact of the omitted pressure term, not a solution of the claimed equations.

failure_location.quote: Therefore, after the time integration stage is completed we projected our solution to a divergence free-vector field using the approach explained in the previous section.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use a standard incompressible integrator: at every step compute the pressure (or apply the discrete Helmholtz projection to the intermediate velocity) so that div v = 0 holds throughout, start from admissible data, and re-run the experiment.
issues.overall_effect: The simulation does not integrate the modified Euler equations and cannot serve as evidence for the obstacle-avoidance claim; the computed trajectory and the reported figures do not represent solutions of (mod:eulereq).
issues.title: Time integration never computes the pressure, so it does not solve the modified Euler equations
issues.why_classification: Adding the per-step pressure solve/projection is a contained standard modification needing no new analysis, but it is a change of numerical method and the specific reported behaviour must be re-established and does not survive for the model as formulated, so more than a purely local edit preserving all claims is required.
